catalog_locator: §7.8 'Stress', pp. 309-317: stress-marking steps (257a-g) pp. 310-311; Table 63 pp. 313-315; rule (261) and fn 168 p. 315; canonical criteria (262), 'unbounded' passage, summary and fns 169-170 p. 316; §7.8.1 phonological word p. 317. 2015 MPhil §5.3.1 p. 88, rule (109c) 'End Rule Right'.
catalog_quote: (g) Observations: H-toned syllables always bear stress. If there is no H tone in a word, the first syllable on the left edge is stressed (i.e., positional prominence, see Hyman 2014b: 70–73). When either an [L] or [M] tone is stressed, the stress is manifested by a slight elevation in pitch and intensity. ... (261) (a) Stress the leftmost [H] tone in a prosodic word (ω). (b) If there are no [H] tones, then stress the leftmost syllable. ... (262) (a) Obligatory: every phonological word (ω) must have a primary stress. (b) Culminative: only one primary stress per ω. (c) Predictable: by rule (261). (d) Autonomous: predictable without grammatical information. (e) Demarcative: calculated from the left edge. (f) Non-moraic: independent of syllable weight. (g) Audible: has phonetic correlates of elevated pitch and intensity. Stress need not be edge-adjacent. It is in this sense unbounded, that is, due to the highest prominence being given to an [H] tone, the main stress does not fall at a fixed distance from the edges (cf. Heinz 2014: 256). ... When a word has more than one [H]-toned syllable, then the leftmost [H] tone bears main stress (End Rule Left). When an [H] tone is lacking, the stress is more subtle. It manifests itself on the leftmost syllable of the stem, in the form of slightly elevated pitch and intensity.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Hrusso Aka has lexical tone (surface H, M, L) and a tone-driven, prominence-based stress system: primary stress falls on the leftmost H-toned syllable of the phonological word; if the word has no H tone, stress defaults to the leftmost (initial, stem) syllable. Stress is obligatory and culminative (one primary stress per phonological word), predictable, computed from the left edge, weight-insensitive, unbounded (not at a fixed distance from an edge), and audible as elevated pitch and intensity; stressed vowels never undergo high-vowel deletion/devoicing.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 316: additional (non-leftmost) [H]-toned syllables 'resemble secondary stress' and are called 'secondary-stressed [H] tones'; primary [H] shows anticipatory F0 slope and post-stress declination even when secondary-stressed [H] tones are present.
new_statements.exceptions: fn 168 p. 315: rule may need to refer to the 'leftmost syllable of the stem', since prefixes do not seem to host stress (fn 170: prefixes bear stress only if H-toned); fn 169: rare stressless monosyllables (e.g. catalog record in table 63) may be clitics. Note the author's own earlier MPhil (2015: 88) analysed main stress as End Rule RIGHT (rightmost H); the 2021 DPhil replaces this with End Rule Left.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (ω), defined in §7.8.1 (p. 317) as the domain of stress and of high-vowel deletion; analysis is of continuous narrated speech (story hru_1241, 102 words, table 63), not citation forms.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Hrusso Aka (community spelling; 'Hruso'/'Hruso Aka' are exonymous spellings), the language of hrus1242, West Kameng district, Arunachal Pradesh; the stress analysis is based on a narrated text recorded at Palizi village (ELAR deposit hru_1241). The thesis (p. 15-16, §1.6.2) notes that Shafer's (1947) 'Hruso A/B dialects' were in fact two languages (Sajolang/Miji and Hrusso Aka) and that Koro Aka (koro1317) is a separate, unrelated language; Nimasow 2017 lists three minor varieties. No dialect restriction stated for the stress rule.

tone_statements.quote: The Hruso Aka language has an unusual phonological structure with many initial consonant clusters or complex onsets, but mainly open syllables. To some degree tone appears to be relevant to the structure of Hruso Aka, but virtually all details of the grammar and phonology require more study before definitive statements can be offered.

tone_statements.quote: This study investigates the relationship between tone and stress in Aka (Hrusso) language, a threatened Tibeto-Burman language spoken by the eponymous indigenous community in Arunachal Pradesh, India. This paper is an exploration of the complex prosodic processes in the language, such as intricate lexical tone interactions, at least five instances of grammatical tone, and tone-stress interaction. Researcher: Dr Vijay D’Souza | Status: Draft revision

sources.note: Ch. 7 'Tone and stress', §7.8 Stress (pp. 309-317): metrical-grid analysis of a narrated text; H-toned syllables always bear stress, the leftmost [H] in the prosodic word takes main stress (End Rule Left), and a word with no [H] stresses its leftmost (stem) syllable; stress is obligatory, culminative, predictable, demarcative from the left edge, non-moraic, audible (elevated pitch and intensity); non-leftmost [H] tones resemble secondary stress; unbounded (not edge-adjacent).
